The thoughtful framers of our Constitution legislated for our country as they found it. Looking upon it with the eyes of statesmen and patriots, they saw all the sources of rapid and wonderful prosperity; but they saw also that various habits, opinions and institutions peculiar to the various portions of so vast a region were deeply fixed. Distinct sovereignties were in actual existence, whose cordial union was essential to the welfare and happiness of all. Between many of them there was, at least to some extent, a real diversity of interests, liable to be exaggerated through sinister designs; they differed in size, in population, in wealth, and in actual and prospective resources and power; they varied in the character of their industry and staple productions, and [in some] existed domestic institutions which, unwisely disturbed, might endanger the harmony of the whole.

We were kids, obviously stupid, but not stupid enough to not ask. The station had zero clear signs about where to stand or board. Just people milling around. A bus pulls up, we ask the driver, “You going to [location]?” He says yes. So we get on.

Several hours later we pull into some stop that was clearly the wrong direction. I mean, not even close. We ask the driver what the hell. He goes, no, this bus was going to [where we ended up], not [location]. Like we’d imagined the whole conversation. It’s around 2 a.m., unfamiliar impoverished part of town, and we don’t know a single person.

Greyhound staff refused a full refund. Best they’d do was partial, even though they’d literally taken us farther from where we were going. We had almost no money, just some change, couldn’t afford new tickets.

We walked to this run-down convenience store and used the outdoor pay phone to call his cousin. He was furious at Greyhound’s incompetence and lack of customer service, said he’d drive the ~5 hours to get us. While we waited, I got bitten by a guard dog. Turns out several had escaped from a nearby construction site after it was broken into and robbed. The convenience-store employee saw it, let us inside even though they were doing window service only because of the late hour, cleaned the bite, and let us use a cellphone to call the cousin again so we didn’t have to wait outside by the pay phone when he arrived.

Never took Greyhound again.

As a Las Vegas resident who sees a lot of shows, I’d strongly recommend this one—it’s easily among the best available. Every seat seems to provide a good view, although be warned: if you sit in the lower levels, you may get splashed. The tickets look expensive, but I’ve never paid full price because locals’ discounts or personal connections have always helped.

I recently went backstage with a friend who knows one of the performers, and seeing the production’s complicated inner workings was fascinating. With all that water, moving equipment, and performers working so close together, it seems like a potentially hazardous setup, yet everything is carefully managed; I’m not aware of accidents happening regularly.

The show is essentially a dream sequence. People who aren’t artistically inclined, or who dislike interpreting abstract work, may not understand the narrative. Still, there are so many performers and simultaneous things happening that it remains thoroughly entertaining. It’s absolutely worth the time and expense.

Just a warning that chargebacks aren’t always as effective as people think. Hotwire charged our party twice for two hotel rooms. Both bookings were for the same person, on the same night, in different cities, and even had exactly the same transaction time. Hotwire refused to issue a refund, so we escalated the matter to our credit-card company. After several months, VISA sent a letter saying the charges would remain valid because Hotwire had submitted evidence that we had made both transactions. The “evidence” was approximately four photocopied screenshots of the booking process, showing someone entering our name and address into form fields, with numerous huge black marker arrows added. It looked completely nonsensical and inadequate, but VISA accepted it anyway.

If you’re considering Hertz—or searching online for a real person in customer service—here’s my experience.

Years ago, an RV hit my unoccupied Hertz rental car while it was parked. The driver left insurance information, but the insurer denied my claim. Hertz didn’t pursue it. Instead, they told me I was responsible for paying for the damage, even though the other driver appeared to be at fault. I boycotted Hertz for eight years.

When I finally rented from them again, my flight was delayed during the widespread confusion over the newly introduced fluids ban. Less than an hour after I arrived, Hertz had given away my reserved car. They had no replacement, so I was stranded in a town where, fortunately, family could help.

After I got home, I sent an angry letter. Hertz basically refused to help.

My blog post about Hertz’s service—and finding an actual human contact—remains one of my most-discovered pages, especially for searches about Hertz’s real customer-service address, which the company seems to hide to discourage direct complaints.

We had planned on seeing "O" when were in Vegas but I think they were on vacation or something. So we decided to give La Reve a shot since it is basically a knock off of O.

We were already staying at Encore so it was a short walk to the theater. We had great seats, 3rd row or so. I think the show has some sort of story, but I had no idea what it was. But that doesn't detract from the enjoyment. Before the show there is a little entertainment in the form of a lizard-like guy that swims around the pool and messes with people in the front rows. At first I thought he was a statue because he'll stay there motionless for a while at times. Then he will sneak up on some unsuspecting theater patron and squirt water at them or something. Pretty funny.

The show is pretty amazing. The pool has platforms in it that raise and lower throughout the show so at times the performers are swimming, diving into the pool or even seemingly walking on water. At one point the performers were diving into the pool from about 25 feet above the water!

So if you want to see a great show and you don't want to pay the astronomical prices for a Cirque de Soleil show, give La Reve a shot.

I really enjoyed this Las Vegas theatrical/circus-style show and would recommend it, though I took off one star. The storyline can be difficult to follow, and a few musical numbers feel sleepy or simply wrong for the action.

The venue is a huge plus: both the auditorium and stage are circular, so every seat provides a good view. The three principal stage entrances are also important, especially during the major transitions in the story.

The performers are seriously impressive, with great physiques, athletic ability, and incredible aerobic skills. The female performers remaining underwater for several minutes is genuinely amazing. The stage, overall setting, and lighting are beautiful. I did wish for more spectacular effects, especially fire, but that isn’t a serious flaw. Ticket prices also seem reasonable compared with major Vegas productions like “O” and “Love.”

Definitely worth seeing if you’re considering a ticket.

Le Rêve means “The Dream,” but good luck sleeping through it—the visuals pull you in too hard for that. It’s not Cirque’s *O*, though both share water, acrobatics, music, and Franco Dragone’s fingerprints. They’re still totally different shows, each worth seeing on its own. The acrobatics, sets, lighting, and water here are flat-out stunning. Honestly, skip the slots and blackjack and spend that money on this instead. You’ll save cash because you can’t count cards while you’re staring at the stage. See *O* once, see *Le Rêve*—then go back again.

My unbiased rating is 4 stars but my biased rating would be somewhere around 2.5-3 stars.

I've never been interested in watching a cirque de soleil show and this is my first one. It had a lot less backflips and crazy acrobatics then i expected....much more interpretive dancing type stuff. Either way the stuff these guys and gals do are very impressive and i'm sure anyone that is a fan of these types of shows would enjoy Le Reve.

Personally i would never pay the 100+ dollars to watch these shows but we got free tickets so yay!

My co-workers and I attended this December after running a half marathon. We got half-price admission through the race and grabbed drinks beforehand. I was excited but tired going in, with high expectations for my first major Las Vegas production.

The circular stage and water arena were utilized effectively, accompanied by impressive strength-based acts. Entertaining moment: a creature resembling the Creature from the Blue Lagoon spit water at people in the front row. However, the plot was unfocused and difficult to follow, especially the connection among the various performers and acts. Fellow travelers and prospective showgoers, I’d intended to see O, but it was on hiatus, so we booked La Rêve instead. We were staying at Encore, making the theater an easy walk away, and our seats were in about the third row. I knew La Rêve is often compared to—possibly even derivative of—O, so I figured it would be a fair substitute. It may not be O, but it’s a solid substitute.

Maybe La Rêve has a story, but I didn’t understand it, and that wasn’t a problem for me. Before the main performance, a comic lizard-like performer swims in the pool, stays still long enough to resemble a statue, then surprises people in the front rows by sneaking up and spraying them with water.

The main spectacle is the draw: a pool with platforms that rise and lower, performers swimming, diving, and appearing to walk on water, plus a dive from roughly 25 feet above the pool. If you want an impressive major Vegas show without Cirque du Soleil’s very high prices, I recommend La Rêve as a worthy alternative. We left impressed.

Papa Johns offers online ordering and delivery to my office, but I think its pizza is horrible. I stopped ordering after the company cut Fry’s hours, along with other employees’ hours, apparently to avoid having to provide health benefits. I’ve since learned about practices there that I find morally objectionable. I used to deliver pizzas, and it’s hard work; the miles also put wear and damage on a driver’s car. I’m not a socialist or a fiscal liberal, but I won’t support Papa Johns. Now I order from locally owned pizzerias. Calling by phone is fine, and their pizza is better.

I visited this unnamed Las Vegas buffet on a Friday at about 4:30 p.m., and fortunately there was no line. The total came to approximately $130 for two people. Before going, I expected the price to be comparable to a steakhouse; afterward, I learned the buffet actually cost somewhat more than that expectation. At that price, I assumed steak would be included, so I was disappointed that it was not offered.

The meat selections included lamb, prime rib, and chicken. They were perfectly acceptable, but I felt these are foods you can find at other Las Vegas buffets for much less money. The seafood station was more interesting, with Alaskan crab legs and rock crab claws. Alaskan crab legs are available at many local buffets, but I had not encountered rock crab claws elsewhere.

Unfortunately, the buffet did not provide crab-claw crackers. When I asked, staff said wooden mallets were available instead. Our table was positioned very close to another table, and I did not want to use a mallet and send pieces of crab shell toward nearby diners. As a result, I ate only the crab legs and skipped the claws.

The Asian station did not seem especially distinctive; it was comparable to the buffet at Rampart Casino. Dessert included gelato and assorted pastries, but nothing stood out. Fresh juices were also available, although I did not try them.

Overall, the buffet was acceptable, but I considered it overpriced for what was offered. If you are curious, it may be worth trying once—especially when there is no wait. However, if you arrive and see a long queue, I would reconsider unless the menu has changed or you particularly want to experience it.

Le Rêve—French for “The Dream”—is one Las Vegas show you won’t sleep through. Franco Dragone’s aquatic spectacle is too visually spectacular and absorbing for that, dazzling with daring acrobatics, surreal sets, dramatic lighting, and a stunning pool-stage. It shares Cirque du Soleil’s O’s water, acrobatics, music, and creator, yet feels completely distinct and uniquely its own. See both; then return to Le Rêve again. Skip slots or blackjack and spend your money here. You can’t count cards while watching, which makes it a genuine savings plan. Immersive, dreamlike, and unforgettable, it’s a must-see Vegas experience.

I’ve been going to Vegas pretty much my whole life—well, the under-21 version of it—so I’ve sat through a lot of shows before I could even gamble. Le Rêve at the Wynn is one I finally caught, and honestly? Mixed. Maybe slightly worse than mixed.

First, the good: the circular stage is genuinely smart. You’re basically looking down into it, so from essentially any seat you get a decent view. That’s rare in Vegas. Some individual acts are impressive too—the strength stuff, the aerialists, the divers. Those people are athletes, no question. But a lot of it reminded me of Cirque du Soleil. Not in a “rip-off” way exactly, just... if you’ve seen Cirque, you’ve seen comparable feats done with maybe more clarity.

And clarity is the problem. What is the story? I still don’t know. There’s a dream, maybe? A guy? Water? It felt like a bunch of pretty images thrown at you, and the show never tells you what it’s trying to say. Also, there’s way too much happening at once. Too many people, too many elements, too many “wow” moments stacked on top of each other. A more restrained production would hit harder. This felt like the stereotypical Vegas spectacle thing—more must be better—so they crammed everything in.

Ticket note: if you’re staying at Wynn or Encore, they have a deal—$99 instead of the normal $125. That helps. Would I see it again? Probably not, and I wouldn’t pay for it a second time. Apart from a few stunts, it was just average. I wasn’t blown away, and I don’t think anyone else was either. That said, a few friends liked it, and if you’ve never seen it, maybe check it out. Just don’t expect to leave overwhelmed.

I agree with Misti Y-- that some people may love the Cirque shows and still dislike *Le Rêve*, although that comparison is really a separate discussion. For me, the theater and visual design are the strongest parts. The scenery and décor are breathtaking from beginning to end, and the whole concept behind the show is beautiful and appealing. Unfortunately, it doesn’t translate very well to the live performance. The storyline isn’t especially entertaining, and when I attended one performance, the stage malfunctioned repeatedly throughout the evening. That made it hard to stay engaged, even during the more impressive scenes. *Le Rêve* seems to be reaching for some of the flair and spectacle associated with Cirque, but it never quite gets there. I’d consider it mainly for the chance to experience that beautiful theater. Otherwise, you might be better off spending your money on another show.

I now live in Toronto and no longer use Hydro Ottawa, but I want to warn other consumers about their alarming billing practices. 

I previously held an account for one year while renting a downtown apartment. When I moved back in with my parents to pursue an MA, I officially cancelled my account and paid all outstanding charges. 

Despite the cancellation, Hydro Ottawa continued siphoning payments from my separate bank account at random intervals for over a year. I repeatedly phoned customer service and sent proof of the withdrawals, but representatives insisted my account was closed and that no debits were occurring. 

The truth emerged only when my parents and I cross-referenced our utility bills: Hydro Ottawa had mistakenly linked my banking details to my parents’ billing number simply because I had mentioned moving home. My parents had not noticed because they frequently received overpayment refunds, making the credits seem normal. 

After hours on the phone and speaking with multiple representatives, a manager finally investigated, confirmed the error, and addressed it. Shockingly, they initially refused a refund and offered only an apology.

Quick take on *Awakening* at Wynn Las Vegas: it’s fine, but not the Vegas must-see I’d build a trip around.

I’ve been taken to Las Vegas constantly since I was a kid—saw a ton of shows before I turned 21—so I’ve got a decent baseline for what these productions can be.

Good news: the circular stage is genuinely smart. From basically any seat, you get a decent view, which is rare in these big theater shows. If you’re staying at Wynn or Encore, there’s a solid deal: tickets normally $125 are $99 for hotel guests. That helps.

Some individual acts are impressive, and the performers are clearly strong as hell—aerialists, acrobats, whatever. But a lot of the feats feel like things I’ve seen done just as well in Cirque du Soleil shows.

The bigger problem is the story. It’s unclear, weak, or practically nonexistent; I left not really knowing what the production was trying to say. There’s also too much going on at once—too many visuals, too many moving pieces, too many “wow” attempts. A more restrained production would hit harder.

Aside from a few cool stunts, the whole thing felt average. I wasn’t blown away, and no one I was with seemed overwhelmed either. A few friends did enjoy it, so if you’ve never seen it, maybe check it out—especially with the Wynn/Encore deal. But I wouldn’t see it again or pay full price a second time. It tries to be the stereotypical huge, flashy Vegas spectacle where more equals better. More just meant messier for me.

Ran the Vegas half marathon this past December, so my coworkers and I got half-price tickets to this. We grabbed a few drinks beforehand and during. It was my first major Vegas production, so expectations were sky-high, even though I was completely exhausted from running.

The setup is pretty neat—circular stage, massive water arena. There’s even a performer resembling the Creature from the Blue Lagoon who spits water right at the front row. A few strength-based acts were genuinely impressive, and the stage/water effects were cool to look at. 

Still, the plot was an unfocused mess and hard to follow. I couldn't see any real connection among the performers, and the central premise just seemed to be a girl undecided about whether to share her life with a boy. 

Ultimately, it was unimpressive and didn't meet my expectations. It might be worth catching at a much deeper discount, but I wouldn't pay half price to go back or take a first-time attendee. Verdict: Skip it.

P.S. Despite what other reviews say, this wasn't advertised as a Cirque du Soleil show; maybe it was associated in the past, but not now.

I agree with Misti Y-- that some people may love Cirque shows and come away disliking *Le Rêve*, although whether Cirque is better is a separate discussion. Having attended one performance of *Le Rêve*, I found the theater and visual design impressive, but the entertainment value was disappointing. The scenery and décor are breathtaking throughout, and the show’s underlying concept is attractive—almost beautiful. Unfortunately, that idea does not translate effectively to the live performance. The storyline is not especially entertaining, and the stage malfunctioned repeatedly during the evening I attended. Each technical problem made it harder to stay engaged and disrupted the momentum the production had. *Le Rêve* seems to borrow, or aspire to, the flair associated with Cirque shows, but it never fully achieves it. I would consider it mainly for the chance to experience the beautiful theater. Otherwise, you may want to spend your money on another show.

I went to this buffet on a Friday around 4:30 p.m., and surprisingly, there was no line at all. Two people came out to about $130, which felt pretty steep. Before going, I figured the price would be comparable to a steakhouse. Afterward, I learned the buffet actually cost somewhat more than what I had expected to pay at one.

Honestly, I was disappointed that steak wasn’t offered. At that price, I assumed there would be some kind of steak option. The meat choices included lamb, prime rib, and chicken, but those are things I feel like you can find at other Las Vegas buffets for much less money.

The seafood station had Alaskan crab legs and rock crab claws. Alaskan crab legs are available at a lot of Vegas buffets, but I hadn’t run into rock crab claws anywhere else, so those were interesting. The problem was that there were no crab-claw crackers. Staff said wooden mallets were available, but our table was so close to the next table that I didn’t want to start smashing crab shells and send pieces flying at the people next to us. So I just ate the crab legs.

The Asian station didn’t seem especially distinctive either. It reminded me quite a bit of the buffet at Rampart Casino. Dessert had gelato and various pastries, but nothing really stood out. They also had fresh juices, although I didn’t try any.

Overall, I’d call the buffet acceptable, but overpriced for what it offers. If you’re curious, it’s worth trying once, especially if there’s no wait. But if the line is long, I’d probably reconsider.

If you’re considering tickets to this Cirque-style show, know the venue has no bad seats. We bought VIP seating, which included chocolates and champagne, plus access to a private monitor showing behind-the-stage and underwater activity. The ushers and hostess gave excellent service. When a loud couple sat nearby, an usher kindly offered to relocate us if the noise became intolerable. Honestly, despite the impressive production elements, I don’t personally enjoy Cirque shows. It felt typical of the genre; viewers who like this type will probably appreciate it. I’ve also seen Mystère and KÀ and would rate all three the same. Still, the performers’ technical feats are impressive.

First major show in Vegas, half off due to being a half marathon participant, I was excited (and tired) to see the show! My co-workers and I gathered, got some drinks, admired the circular stage, laughed at the creature from the blue lagoon spitting water at folks in the front row, and then became very bewildered from there...

The story line is a bit unfocused and hard to follow, never quite sure how the different actors/pieces fit into what was originally introduced as the girl's indecision to share her life with the boy or not....

Some neat acts of strength, nice use of the stage and water arena, but all in all, this show just didn't impress me. I think I was just expecting so much more from a Vegas show and had higher hopes than what was presented. Again, a clear understanding of the storyline would've helped as well.

Verdict: Interesting show. For a deeper discount, I'd consider going back, but even at half price, I'm not sure I'd be willing to watch it again or bring anyone that hasn't been there before. Ah well.

P.S. This is not a Cirque du Soleil show, despite what many Yelpers have written. It may have been in the past, but as of December when I visited, it definitely is not advertised as such...

Aluminum conducts heat better than cast iron, meaning heat moves through it faster. That is why a thin aluminum pan heats up quickly and responds fast when you raise or lower the burner. But staying hot is not just about conductivity. It also depends on how much heat the pan can store.

A cast-iron pan is usually much thicker and heavier than a thin aluminum pan. Because it has more mass, it can hold a larger amount of heat energy. Once it is hot, adding cold food does not cool it down as quickly. The thin aluminum pan may transfer heat efficiently, but it has less stored heat to give.

For example, if you sear a cold steak, a hot cast-iron skillet often keeps sizzling after the steak hits the surface. A thin aluminum pan may lose temperature quickly, so the steak can steam or gray before browning well.

One limitation of the comparison is that pan design matters. A thick aluminum pan, especially one with a heavy base, can hold heat much better than a very thin one. So the difference is not only the metal, but also the pan’s thickness, weight, and construction.

Aluminum is great at moving heat, but that’s not the same as holding a lot of heat.

Think of heat like money. Aluminum is a fast spender: it takes heat from the burner and passes it along quickly to the food. Cast iron is more like a thick savings account. It takes longer to heat up because there’s so much heavy metal to warm, but once it’s hot, it has stored a lot of energy. So when you drop in a cold steak, a handful of mushrooms, or a wet batch of zucchini, the cast-iron pan’s temperature doesn’t crash as fast.

That’s why a cast-iron skillet can give you better browning on a steak. The meat pulls heat from the pan immediately, and the pan has enough thermal mass to keep searing instead of cooling down and steaming the surface. A thin aluminum pan may heat quickly, but it can lose temperature quickly too, especially if the food is cold or crowded.

One limitation: this comparison depends on thickness and construction. A thick aluminum pan, especially one with a heavy base, can hold plenty of heat, while a small, thin cast-iron pan won’t feel magically powerful. Conductivity matters; it’s just not the whole story.

Aluminum conducts heat better than cast iron, so heat moves through an aluminum pan more quickly. That helps the pan respond fast when you turn the burner up or down. But staying hot is not just about how fast heat moves. It also depends on how much heat the pan can store.

A typical cast-iron skillet is much thicker and heavier than a thin aluminum pan. That extra mass acts like a heat reservoir. Once it is fully preheated, it contains more stored heat, so its temperature drops more slowly when you add cold food.

For example, put a room-temperature steak in a hot cast-iron skillet and in a thin aluminum pan. The steak pulls heat out of both pans. The thin aluminum pan may transfer heat into the steak quickly at first, but it has less stored heat, so its surface temperature can fall fast. The cast iron may conduct heat less efficiently, but because it is heavy, it can keep feeding heat into the steak and maintain a stronger sear.

One limitation: this comparison depends on the actual pans. A thick aluminum griddle can store plenty of heat, and a small, thin cast-iron pan may not. Burner size and preheating time also matter.

In cooking, though, the issue is often not just how fast heat moves, but how much the pan’s temperature drops when cold food hits it.

Cast iron is usually much thicker and heavier than a thin aluminum pan. That extra mass gives it more thermal mass: it stores more heat energy once it has been preheated. When you add cold food, there is more stored heat available at the cooking surface, so the pan resists cooling down as quickly. A thin aluminum pan may transfer heat efficiently, but it has less stored heat to give up.

For example, if you put a cold steak in a well-preheated cast-iron skillet, it often keeps sizzling after the meat hits the surface. In a thin aluminum pan, the surface may lose temperature quickly, and the steak can steam or turn gray before it browns well.

One limitation is that this is not only about the metal. A thick aluminum pan with a heavy base can hold heat much better than a very thin one, and burner power, preheating, and construction all matter.

I bought this second-hand mechanical keyboard for $38, so I wasn’t expecting perfection, and that is pretty much what I got. It arrived reasonably clean and worked right away, which was a relief. The typing feel is actually better than I expected for the price. I write a lot of long emails for work, and the keys are comfortable enough that my hands don’t feel tired after an hour or two.

There are a couple of issues, though. The space bar rattles noticeably, especially if I hit it near the edges, and it makes the whole board sound cheaper than it feels. Also, one key occasionally repeats, which is annoying when I’m typing quickly and have to go back to delete an extra letter. It doesn’t happen constantly, but it happens enough to mention.

The seller did answer my question about the switches, but it took a full week, by which point I had basically figured it out myself. I considered returning it, but for $38, shipping it back didn’t seem worth the trouble. Overall, I kept it because it is comfortable and usable, just not flawless.

At 3:12 every Thursday morning, Mara found the book on the flour bin.

It was always the same one: The Atlas of Vanished Islands, wrapped in a blue library jacket, its due-date card stamped so often the ink had become a bruise. She would set it by the till before dawn, and by noon someone from the library would come collect it with a sigh and a clipboard.

Tonight, while the first trays of cardamom buns breathed in the oven, Mara lifted the cover and found a note tucked at page 47.

Please don’t send it back yet. I think the island on this page is where my mother said she was born. She died last winter. I don’t know who else to ask.

Mara stood very still, dusted white to the elbows, while the mixer thumped behind her like a second heart. Outside, rain polished the empty street. Page 47 showed a crescent of land no bigger than a thumbnail, gone beneath the sea in 1891.

At five, she took a warm bun from the rack, slid the note beneath it, and placed both in the bakery window.

At 2:17 every Thursday morning, Mara found the library book on the bakery’s back step.

Always the same one: A Field Guide to North American Moths, county library sticker ghost-pale on the spine, a little flour worked into the jacket as if the book had been helping. She’d returned it twice. The librarians smiled too politely. By the third week, she kept it beside the rye starter and said nothing.

Tonight, rain ticked against the alley door. The ovens breathed. Mara was shaping croissants, palms pressing butter into dough, when the latch gave its tiny, guilty click.

No one there. Just the book, dry as a bone on the wet concrete.

She wiped her hands on her apron and opened it. A slip of paper lay between “Luna Moth” and “Promethea,” folded once.

Your window is the only light on this street. I read here until the first bus. I’m sorry about the crumbs.

Mara looked at the alley, at the dented milk crates and the steam rising off the drains. The city felt enormous for a second, then not.

She tore a corner from an order pad and wrote, Cinnamon rolls come out at 4:05.

Then she set the note inside the book, placed it on the warm windowsill, and unlocked the back door.

At 3:12 every Thursday morning, Mara found the book in the bread rack.

It was always the same one: The Practical Guide to Inland Birds, cracked blue spine, library stamp from a town forty miles away. She would set it on the flour bin, wipe butter from the cover, and mean to take it back after her shift. By noon, the errands and heat and sleep would swallow the thought.

Then, next Thursday, there it would be again, tucked between cooling rye loaves.

Tonight the bakery hummed with the proofing cabinet and the old radio’s static. Rain pressed silver lines down the front window. Mara lifted the book with both hands, as if it might be warm.

A folded receipt marked the chapter on herons.

She opened it.

In block letters, someone had written: I THINK YOU ARE THE ONLY PERSON AWAKE WHEN I AM. PAGE 47.

Mara turned to page 47. A grey heron stood in a marsh, one foot raised, patient as a saint. Under the picture, in pencil: THURSDAY, 3:30?

The clock over the mixer clicked once.

Mara brushed flour from her apron, unlocked the front door, and turned on the little OPEN sign.

At 3:12 every Thursday morning, Mara found the book on the flour bin.

It was always the same one: The Atlas of Vanished Islands, wrapped in a blue library jacket, its due-date card stamped until the boxes ran together. She set it by the till before dawn, and by noon Mr. Pelham from the library would come for it, tapping his pen twice on the counter before he signed.

Tonight, with cardamom buns browning on the middle rack and sesame loaves waiting under damp cloth, Mara opened the cover. A note was folded into page 47.

Please don’t send it back yet. My mother said she was born on Saint Orla, but this says it vanished in 1891. She died last winter. Did people use the old name for somewhere else? There’s a harbor mark here like the one on her bracelet.

Mara read it twice. Flour had dried in the crack of her thumb. The mixer was off for once, and the bakery made small noises: cooling metal, rain in the alley drain, yeast tubs ticking under their lids.

At five, she tore a square from a pastry bag, wrote, Come after closing, took one warm bun from the rack, and set book, note, and bun in the front window.

Aluminum conducts heat faster, but staying hot depends on a different property: how much heat a pan can store. That's heat capacity, and it depends on how much material you have. A cast-iron skillet is thick and heavy, often 4 to 5 pounds, while a thin aluminum pan might weigh under a pound. Even though aluminum itself holds more heat per pound than iron, the cast-iron pan has far more mass, so it stores much more total heat.

Conductivity mostly affects how quickly and evenly heat spreads. Aluminum heats up fast and responds quickly when you turn the burner down, which also means it loses heat quickly once food hits it.

Here's a kitchen example: you preheat both pans to the same temperature and lay in two cold steaks. The thin aluminum pan's temperature drops sharply because it has little stored heat to give up, and the steaks may start to steam instead of sear. The cast-iron pan dips less, recovers faster, and keeps browning.

One limitation: this comparison isn't perfectly fair if the pans differ in size, thickness, or burner contact. A thick aluminum pan could store plenty of heat too, and cast iron can develop hot spots because it spreads heat less evenly.

Here's the thing people get tangled up on: conducting heat and holding heat are two different jobs. Aluminum is a fantastic conductor, so heat zips through it fast. But it's also light, and a light pan simply doesn't have much stuff in it to store energy. Cast iron is a mediocre conductor, yet it's heavy, and all that mass acts like a battery. More iron means more stored heat.

Picture dropping two cold steaks into two pans that were both preheated to the same temperature. The thin aluminum pan heats up evenly in seconds, but the moment cold meat hits it, the temperature plunges, and there's not much reserve to bounce back. You get gray, steamy edges. The cast-iron pan dips a little, too, but it has so much stored heat to draw on that the surface stays hot enough to build a real crust. That's why I'll always grab iron for searing (and why my aluminum skillet is relegated to eggs).

The limitation? Iron's slow conduction means it heats unevenly. Put it on a small burner and you'll get a hot spot in the middle while the edges lag, so you've got to preheat patiently. Heavy doesn't automatically mean better.

Two properties are in play, and they pull in different directions. Conductivity is how fast heat moves through the metal. Heat capacity is how much heat the metal holds at a given temperature. Aluminum wins on the first. Cast iron wins on the second, mostly because a typical skillet is far heavier.

A 10-inch cast-iron skillet weighs around five pounds. A thin aluminum pan of the same width might weigh one. At the same temperature, the iron pan stores several times more heat, simply because there is more metal to store it in.

Now put a cold steak on each. The aluminum pan spreads heat evenly and quickly, but it has little in reserve. The steak pulls heat out, the pan's surface temperature drops, and the burner has to catch up. The iron pan's surface dips less, because the thick body keeps feeding heat to the steak. That is why the sear stays hard and the crust browns instead of the meat turning gray and steaming.

The limitation: cast iron conducts poorly, so it heats unevenly. A small burner leaves a hot spot under the flame and cooler edges. Staying hot is not the same as heating evenly.

Aluminum is the better conductor, but staying hot is a different job. It comes down to how much heat the metal can hold, which is its mass multiplied by how much heat each pound absorbs. Per pound, aluminum actually holds more heat than iron. Per cubic inch, the two are close. So the deciding factor is simply how much metal is in the pan.

A 10-inch cast-iron skillet usually weighs about 4 to 5 pounds. A thin aluminum pan of the same size may weigh well under a pound. The skillet carries several times more stored heat at the same temperature.

Picture both pans preheated to the same temperature, then two cold, damp steaks laid in each. The thin aluminum pan gives up its small reserve almost at once, and its surface temperature falls fast. Juices pool instead of evaporating, and the steaks start to steam. The skillet dips too, but less, because it has so much heat to spend, so the surface stays hot enough to keep browning.

Conductivity plays a different role. It governs how quickly heat spreads across the pan, which is why aluminum heats fast and cast iron feels slow.

The comparison has a limit: it assumes thin aluminum. A thick, heavy aluminum pan can hold heat nearly as well as cast iron.

Marguerite found the book where she always did on Thursdays: wedged between the flour bins and the cooling racks, as if it had climbed in through the wall. *A Field Guide to Coastal Birds*, spine cracked, a faded library stamp inside the cover. Due date long past.

Eleven Thursdays now. She'd asked the day staff, checked the locks, even stayed late once with a thermos and a rolling pin. Nothing. The book simply appeared between two and four a.m., and she never caught the moment.

Tonight it was heavier. She opened it and a folded square of receipt paper slid out.

*I keep meaning to bring it back to the library, but I walk past your window on the way and the light is on, and I think: somebody is awake. Then I leave it here instead. Sorry. I'll stop if you ask me to.*

Marguerite read it twice. Behind her the ovens ticked, and the first trays of rye waited under their cloths.

She turned the receipt over, found a pencil stub behind her ear, and wrote on the back: *Don't stop.* Then she tucked it inside the cover, set the book on the sill by the front window, and left the light on.

Dov reads it twice. Then a third time, mostly to the part about the street.

He pulls a pencil from behind his ear, flips the note over, and writes: *Back door's open at 4. Bread's free.*

Then he props the door with a brick.

Think of a cast-iron pan as a heavy, slow-moving cargo ship, and a thin aluminum pan as a nimble speedboat. Even though aluminum conducts heat quickly—meaning it warms up and cools down almost instantly—it lacks the physical mass to store that energy. Cast iron is incredibly dense and heavy. It takes longer to heat up, but once it does, it holds onto that thermal energy like a giant battery.

For a concrete kitchen example, imagine searing a cold, thick ribeye steak. When you drop that cold meat into a thin aluminum pan, the pan’s temperature plummets instantly, causing the steak to steam in its own juices rather than sear. If you drop that same steak into a hot cast-iron skillet, the heavy pan barely registers the cold meat; it retains its intense heat, instantly creating a beautifully caramelized, deep-brown crust.

One limitation of this comparison is that it ignores pan thickness. A incredibly thick, heavy-gauge aluminum pan (like professional cookware) will hold heat much better than a cheap, paper-thin one, though heavy cast iron will still reign supreme in heat retention due to its sheer density.

Of course, this comparison isn't perfect. We’re comparing heavy-duty cast iron to thin, cheap aluminum. A super-thick, professional-grade aluminum pan would hold heat much better, though it still wouldn’t match the sheer heat-retaining muscle of iron.

The iron pumps stored energy back into the meat, instantly vaporizing moisture to create a deep, brown crust.

At 3:17 a.m., the bakery was all yeast and silence. Marisol slid the first loaves into the oven and found it again: a worn paperback, *The Borrowers*, resting in the wicker basket by the back door. Every Thursday for six weeks, someone had returned it here instead of the library two blocks over. No name. No card. Just the book, smelling faintly of rain and woodsmoke.

Tonight a folded note was tucked between pages 84 and 85. She wiped her floury hands and opened it. *I can't make it to the library before closing. Please keep it another week. I like knowing it's warm.*

Marisol looked at the basket, then at the tray of cinnamon rolls cooling on the rack. She chose the one with the most icing. She wrapped it in wax paper, tucked the note back into the book, and set both by the door. Then she flipped the sign to OPEN and started the coffee.

At 3:47 a.m. the book was there again. Same one—a battered copy of The Long Winter—resting on the flour bin like it had walked in and made itself comfortable. Every Thursday, without fail. I’d stopped asking who. The regulars were asleep. The mice don’t read.

I wiped my hands and opened the cover. A note, folded twice, smelled faintly of cinnamon. Not my cinnamon. I unfolded it.

You always leave the oven light on. It helps.

That was it. No name. No reason. I stood there with dough stuck to my knuckles, listening to the proof box hum. Outside, a bus sighed past. I thought about the woman who buys a single roll every Friday and never eats it in front of me. I thought about my mother’s handwriting, which this wasn’t.

Then I slid the note into my apron pocket, tucked the book under the register, and pulled the next tray of croissants from the oven.

At 2:40 a.m., while the ovens clicked through their preheat, Marla found the book again. *The Anatomy of Melancholy*, stamped with the county library’s faded crest, sitting on the flour bin like a delivered loaf. Every Thursday. No one saw who left it. The security camera showed only the alley, rain, a shadow that didn’t resolve.

She wiped her hands and opened the cover. This time a note lay against the title page, folded twice. Blue ink, block letters: *You burned the last batch. I did too.* No signature.

Marla read it once. The proofing dough breathed under its cloth. She looked at the alley door, the small window, the dark. Then she slid the note into her apron pocket, set the book on the cooling rack beside the day-old rye, and turned back to the mixer. She poured in the water, started the paddle, and watched the dry flour pull away from the bowl’s sides.

At 3:17 a.m., Marisol heard the walk-in cooler kick on and the proofing cabinet breathe. She slid the first loaves into the oven. In the wicker basket by the back door sat the worn paperback again: *The Borrowers*. For six Thursdays someone had left it here instead of the library two blocks over. The checkout card in back was blank; only a barcode and a coffee ring marked it.

A folded note was tucked between pages 84 and 85. She wiped her hands on her apron and read: *I can’t get to the library before it closes. Please keep it here another week. I like knowing it’s warm.*

She looked at the basket, then at the tray of cinnamon rolls cooling on the rack. She chose the one with the most icing, wrapped it in wax paper, and tucked the note back into the book. She set both by the door. At 4:50 she pulled the loaves, knocked them from their pans, and slid the next tray into the oven.

It might seem counterintuitive that a cast-iron skillet retains heat longer than a thin aluminum pan, given that aluminum is actually a superior thermal conductor. The key difference lies in thermal mass and specific heat capacity, not just conductivity. Cast iron is significantly denser and heavier than thin aluminum. This means it can store a much larger amount of thermal energy for any given temperature. When you place a cold steak into the pan, the cast iron has a vast reservoir of stored heat to draw from, preventing the surface temperature from dropping drastically. In contrast, a thin aluminum pan has very little mass. While it heats up quickly due to high conductivity, it also loses its stored energy rapidly when faced with a cold ingredient, leading to uneven cooking or steaming rather than searing.

Consider searing a thick ribeye steak. A preheated cast-iron skillet will maintain a consistent, high surface temperature throughout the process, creating a perfect, crispy crust. A thin aluminum pan would likely cool down too much upon contact, resulting in a gray, boiled exterior instead of a desirable Maillard reaction. However, this comparison has a limitation: it assumes the aluminum pan is thin. If you were to compare cast iron to a thick, heavy-bottomed aluminum roasting pan, the aluminum might actually retain heat quite well due to its increased mass, narrowing the performance gap significantly. Therefore, thickness and total mass are just as critical as the material itself when evaluating heat retention capabilities in your kitchen tools.

Look, it’s totally counterintuitive, right? We’re taught that aluminum is the speed demon of the kitchen, whisking heat away from the burner faster than you can say "sauté." And it is. But there’s a massive difference between moving heat quickly and actually holding onto it. Think of it like this: aluminum is a sprinter, while cast iron is a marathon runner with a heavy backpack.

The secret sauce here is thermal mass. Cast iron is dense and thick. It takes a long time to heat up because it needs to soak up a ton of energy, but once it’s hot, it’s got a serious reservoir of thermal energy stored up. Aluminum pans are usually thin and light; they heat up instantly but lose that energy just as fast when you drop in a cold steak.

Picture searing a ribeye. If you use a flimsy aluminum pan, the temperature plummets the second the meat hits the surface, leading to steaming instead of searing. The cast iron? It barely blinks. It dumps its stored heat into the steak, giving you that perfect, crusty exterior.

However, don’t get it twisted. This comparison has a limit: we’re mostly talking about standard, thin-gauge aluminum cookware. If you were using a thick, high-end aluminum core pan, the gap narrows significantly because that extra material adds mass. But for your everyday cheap skillet? Iron wins the endurance test every time.

Aluminum conducts heat rapidly, moving thermal energy from the burner to the food quickly. Cast iron conducts heat poorly, resisting that flow. Yet cast iron stays hot longer because it holds more total energy. This property is called heat capacity. A thick block of cast iron contains far more mass than a thin sheet of aluminum. It requires significantly more energy to raise its temperature, but once heated, it releases that stored energy slowly. Aluminum loses its heat almost as fast as it gains it because it has low mass and high conductivity.

Consider searing a steak. You preheat both pans on high heat. When you place the cold meat on the thin aluminum pan, the surface temperature drops instantly. The aluminum cannot replenish the lost heat fast enough from the burner alone. The steak steams instead of searing. The cast iron pan, however, acts like a thermal battery. Its massive reservoir of stored heat buffers the temperature drop. The surface remains hot enough to create a proper crust despite the cold protein touching it.

This comparison has a limitation. It assumes the aluminum pan is thin. A heavy, thick-bottomed aluminum pan or a clad stainless steel pot with an aluminum core can mimic the heat retention of cast iron by increasing mass. The material matters, but the volume of metal determines how much energy is actually stored. Thinness defeats aluminum’s potential for retention, while thickness grants cast iron its staying power.

Aluminum conducts heat faster, yet cast iron holds it longer. This paradox stems from density, not conductivity. Cast iron is heavy. It packs more mass into the same volume than thin aluminum, creating a massive thermal reservoir. While aluminum’s specific heat per gram is actually higher, its low density means a thin pan lacks the total bulk to store significant energy. Cast iron’s sheer weight compensates, allowing it to hoard heat.

Drop a cold ribeye onto a preheated thin aluminum sheet. The temperature plummets. The steak steams in its own juices, turning gray and sad. No deep browning occurs. Now try cast iron. The skillet barely flinches. Its stored energy overwhelms the cold meat, maintaining the high surface heat needed for a rich, dark crust. The difference is immediate and visual.

But do not mistake material for destiny. Thickness matters. A heavy-bottomed aluminum roasting pan rivals cast iron because its increased mass bridges the gap. If you compare equal weights, the playing field levels. The common kitchen comparison fails because it pits heavy iron against flimsy aluminum. When evaluating your cookware, look beyond the metal type. Check the heft. A thick layer of any metal will outperform a thin one, regardless of conductivity. For searing, you need mass to buffer the shock of cold food. Aluminum can do this, but only if it is built thick enough to carry the load.

Conductivity and heat storage are two different things. Conductivity describes how quickly heat moves through a material. Aluminum excels at this, so a thin aluminum pan heats fast and spreads heat evenly. Staying hot, however, depends on how much heat the pan has stored, and that depends mostly on mass. A typical cast-iron skillet weighs five or six pounds, while a thin aluminum pan might weigh one. Even though aluminum stores more heat per pound than iron, the heavy skillet holds far more heat in total.

Picture searing four cold steaks. When they hit a thin aluminum pan, they pull heat out faster than the burner can replace it. The surface temperature drops, the meat releases moisture, and the steaks steam and turn gray. Drop the same steaks into a preheated cast-iron skillet and the large reserve of stored heat keeps the surface hot enough to brown them into a deep crust. That same reserve is why cast iron stays warm on the table long after you turn off the stove.

The comparison has a limitation. It really pits a heavy pan against a light one rather than iron against aluminum. A thick aluminum pan of similar weight would hold comparable heat and spread it more evenly, while cast iron tends to develop hot spots over the burner.

Here's the thing people mix up: conducting heat and *holding* heat aren't the same job. Conductivity is about how fast heat moves through metal. Staying hot is about how much heat the pan has stored up, and that depends mostly on mass.

A thin aluminum skillet might weigh a pound. A 12-inch cast-iron pan? Closer to eight. Even though iron stores less heat per ounce than aluminum (about half, honestly), all that extra metal adds up to a much bigger reservoir of energy. Aluminum's great conductivity just means it spreads heat quickly, and it gives it away quickly too.

You've probably felt this. Drop two cold steaks into a ripping-hot thin pan and the sizzle collapses into a sad hiss; the meat drains the heat faster than the burner can replace it, so you get gray, steamed edges. Do the same in preheated cast iron and the sizzle barely flinches. There's enough stored heat to keep searing while the burner catches up. (This is also why cast iron takes forever to preheat, so it's the same trait working against you.)

The limitation: this compares a heavy pan to a light one, not iron to aluminum. A thick, heavy aluminum pan would hold heat just fine, and pound for pound it'd actually win.

At 3:40 a.m., while the second batch of rye was proofing, Marisol found it again: a library book on the flour bin by the back door, its plastic jacket cold from the alley.

Fourth Thursday running. Same book, *A Field Guide to Night Birds*, stamped Eastgate Branch and due three weeks ago. Each time, she'd carried it to the drop box on her way home. Each Thursday it came back, as if the building itself had borrowed it.

She wiped her hands on her apron and opened it. A folded index card slid out from the page on barn owls.

*You leave the vent fan on. The alley smells like bread until five. I walk my mother's dog then, because she can't anymore. I keep forgetting to return this. Maybe I keep not wanting to. —R.*

Marisol read it twice while the oven timer counted down. Outside, the fan hummed, pushing warm air into the dark.

She turned the card over. With the grease pencil she used for marking trays, she wrote: *Rye's out at 4:15.* Then she tore a heel from yesterday's loaf, wrapped it in wax paper, set the book on top, and propped the back door open one inch.

Thursdays, the book shows up. Not on the counter, mind you, but wedged behind the flour bins by the back door, like whoever leaves it knows exactly where I won't trip over it.

It's always the same one: *A Field Guide to North American Moths*, Elmwood Branch, due date stamped so long ago the ink's gone violet. I've never seen anyone drop it off. I'm elbow-deep in rye dough by two, and honestly, at that hour I wouldn't notice a marching band.

The first few weeks I just set it on the shelf by the register. By Friday morning it was gone. Thursday, back again. Fine. People are strange. I'm a guy who talks to his sourdough starter, so I'm not judging.

Tonight there's a note tucked at page 114, the luna moths.

*They only live a week. They don't even eat. I keep thinking that's a waste of a beautiful thing. Do you ever get to see the bread before it's gone?*

No signature. Just pencil, pressed hard.

I read it twice, then a third time while the ovens ticked. Then I pulled the first loaf of the night, still crackling, wrapped it in brown paper, and set it behind the flour bins.

At 2:40 the proofing cabinet clicked off, and Dana went to the back door for the milk crates. The book was on top of them again, in a bread bag knotted at the neck.

Fourth Thursday. Same book: a water-stained copy of *Edible Mushrooms of the Pacific Northwest*, property of the Alder Street branch, due date stamped in purple twelve years ago. The first time, she'd put it in the lost-and-found bin. The second time, she'd driven it to the library's return slot. It came back anyway, on the crates, before dawn.

Tonight a square of lined paper stuck out of chapter six, near the photograph of a chanterelle.

*You open at 6. They open at 10. I can't wait that long. Can you give it to Marguerite at the desk? Tell her I didn't pick the wrong ones.*

No name. The handwriting leaned hard to the right, like it was walking into wind.

Dana read it twice, then set the book on the shelf above the flour bins, where nothing got wet. She pulled a pencil from behind her ear, turned the note over, and wrote: *Which ones did you pick?* She tucked it back into chapter six and left the bread bag on the crates, open.

Cities should create protected bike lanes because they offer safer, cleaner, and more accessible transportation options. Protected bike lanes are those that are physically separated from vehicle traffic by barriers, planters, or curbs, providing a convenient and safe alternative to driving without having to sacrifice convenience and safety. This is particularly important for vulnerable groups such as children, the elderly, or those who might feel uneasy about riding next to vehicles.

Additionally, creating protected bike lanes can help to alleviate traffic congestion and air pollution. Encouraging more people to bike for shorter distances can lead to fewer cars on congested roads, and less greenhouse gases and pollutants released into the atmosphere. Biking also encourages physical activity, which can improve public health and lower the cost of sedentary lifestyles. Protected bike lanes can also often be installed more quickly and at a lower cost than large-scale highway construction projects, making them a cost-effective investment in urban infrastructure.

As seen in Paris, which expanded its cycle paths by over 1,000 kilometers, bike trips nearly doubled (based on city counts) between 2019 and 2022. This shows that people will opt for bikes if they have connected and convenient and protected routes available. It's not just about having a few isolated lanes, but connected networks from home to school, work, stores, and transit.

While some may claim that bike lanes take away space from cars or parking, streets are a shared public space and should be designed to serve the needs of the community as a whole, not just cars. By investing in protected bike lanes, cities can provide safer streets, cleaner air, healthier citizens, and a more sustainable transportation system.

Remote work is heralded as the panacea. From my two years of mentoring 5 junior engineers, it's overblown for any juniors still learning how to code.

Jrs don't need tickets or documentation or meeting. They need to sit in on design conversations. They need to see how others debug issues. They need to ask questions before they have hours of confusion. That kind of interaction happens organically in an office. For remote work, they need to know the right times to cut in, set up a call, and to explain a problem that they might not even fully understand yet. It's a skill (and a tough one!) to have before you have a chance to learn it.

I've seen the feedback issues in remote work. Short comments on code review can feel like the final word instead of a learning opportunity. Also, it takes longer, so less momentum. The jrs I mentored typically improved faster if they had in person pairing, whiteboard sessions, etc. and had easy access to seniors.

I'm not trying to push for offices or anti-flexibility. Remote work can be great for self-driven devs. But for jrs, proximity is a booster that gives confidence, context, and instincts. Sending jrs off with a laptop and a calendar can be a drag on junior development which can result in less good technical leadership in the future.

You could get a whole novel for sixpence. That was the trick Allen Lane pulled off in 1935 when he set up Penguin Books. The price was the same as a packet of cigarettes, and the books looked like it, with colored bands on the spine to sort out the genres. You got the same sort of thing you'd find in a more expensive shop. Some of it was popular fiction, some of it was pretty serious work. That mix did a lot to get rid of the notion that a cheap book had to be a bad one. You'd already seen the shape of the thing in the pamphlets and chapbooks of the past, and in the yellowbacks of the nineteenth century. But the modern version needed the whole package of mass printing, better paper, and a lot more people who could read. It got into the hands of people on the train, in the classroom, and just out for a walk.

The habit caught on fast, first in Britain and then in the United States and other places. That was mostly during and after the Second World War. The printers cranked out the novels, the biographies, the mysteries and romances, and the school books. A soldier, a student, or a working person could put together a library that way. Nobody else could have afforded the same collection. By the middle of the last century that had become the main way people got hold of books. You've still got it to hand now. The electronic versions have not quite managed to displace it. People still want the thing they can pick up and carry around.

You're not alone on this. I got a real soaking on Tuesday and by Thursday half my Brandywines had let go. You can see the seam running right down the side of the fruit. It's the old story of a dry spell followed by a sudden deluge. The inside of the fruit takes in water faster than the skin can stretch to keep up. The Sungolds are mostly holding out so far but I've got a few of those looking like they might follow.

You can't really get around the weather once it's happened. The only thing that helps a bit is keeping that two day schedule you've got on a more even footing. It doesn't matter much in the end though once the sky decides to let it all out at once. You'll likely get a fair crop from the rest of the vines. Just pick the split ones off and put them to some other use.

It's a lot more of a headache with the Brandywines. That thick skin they have is a real liability in a storm like this. You might get better luck with the Sungolds if you can keep them from getting quite so much water in a single go.

The Vogel-Fulcher-Tammann law accurately describes critical slowing in bulk polymer glasses, but it lacks an agreed microscopic theory. We derive it from quantum mechanical transition rates, using the logarithm of final-state phase space as the activation entropy. Closed polymer chains are counted as self-avoiding polygons, while open chains anchored to surfaces are treated separately. For uniform connectivity and Flory-type scaling, the resulting activation entropy has the required energy singularity, giving the VFT form. Surface proximity lowers the dynamical singularity temperature, so films only a few nanometers thick no longer strictly obey the empirical bulk law.

text: A room can feel stuffy even at a comfortable temperature because temperature is only one part of comfort. High humidity slows the evaporation of moisture from skin, making the air feel heavy and stale. Low airflow matters too: without movement, exhaled carbon dioxide, odors, and heat linger near occupants instead of dispersing. Poor ventilation traps these byproducts, so the space feels close and oppressive. Air conditioning may cool the air but not necessarily reduce humidity or improve circulation. Opening a window, using a fan, or running ventilation can restore a fresher feel by moving air and lowering moisture.
task: Explain why a room can feel stuffy even when the temperature is comfortable. Discuss humidity and airflow without giving medical advice.

text: A room may feel stuffy despite a comfortable temperature primarily due to poor ventilation and elevated humidity levels. When airflow is stagnant, carbon dioxide exhaled by occupants accumulates, creating a sense of heaviness or dullness in the air. Simultaneously, high humidity prevents sweat from evaporating efficiently from the skin, which can make the environment feel clammy and oppressive even if the thermometer reads pleasantly. Without adequate circulation from fans, open windows, or HVAC systems, fresh oxygen fails to replace depleted air. This combination of moisture retention and lack of movement disrupts thermal comfort, leading to that characteristic stifling sensation. Improving air exchange effectively mitigates these issues by balancing moisture and replenishing oxygen.

text: A room can feel stuffy even when the temperature is comfortable because “comfort” depends on more than heat. High humidity makes the air feel heavy and can slow the evaporation of moisture from skin, so the space may feel clammy or stale. Low airflow also contributes: when air is not moving or being replaced, odors, moisture, and exhaled air can build up, creating a closed-in feeling. Even at a pleasant temperature, a room with poor ventilation may seem less fresh. Opening a window, using a fan, or improving air circulation can make the same temperature feel much more comfortable.
task: Explain why a room can feel stuffy even when the temperature is comfortable. Discuss humidity and airflow without giving medical advice.

text: A room can feel stuffy even at a comfortable temperature because comfort depends on more than heat. Humidity matters: when the air holds a lot of moisture, sweat evaporates from your skin more slowly, so the air feels heavy, sticky, and close. Airflow matters too. In still air, a thin layer of warm, moist air tends to cling around your body, and without a breeze to carry it away, the space feels stagnant. Poor ventilation can also let cooking smells, dust, and other odors linger, reinforcing that "used air" impression. Opening a window, running a fan, or using a dehumidifier or exhaust vent often makes the room feel fresher without changing the temperature.
task: Explain why a room can feel stuffy even when the temperature is comfortable. Discuss humidity and airflow without giving medical advice.

text:
A room can feel incredibly stuffy even at a comfortable temperature due to high humidity and a lack of airflow. 

When relative humidity is high, the air is saturated with moisture. This slows down the rate at which sweat evaporates from your skin, preventing your body's natural cooling process and making the air feel thick and heavy. 

Without active airflow, this stagnant air traps heat, moisture, and carbon dioxide in a localized "envelope" around your body. Without a breeze or ventilation to disperse these elements, the air becomes stale. Essentially, stagnant, moisture-laden air prevents your skin from breathing, turning a thermally comfortable room into a suffocating environment.

To all Enron employees,

These are difficult days, I know. Between the problems we’re facing inside Enron and the troubling events in the world around us, this holiday season doesn’t feel much like a holiday.

We talked a lot about whether to go ahead with the all-Enron holiday party scheduled for December 8. People felt differently. Some thought it would be a good chance for Enron employees to come together and celebrate. Others felt it just wasn’t appropriate right now. I understand both views.

text:
A float valve connects the trough to a pressurized water line. A buoyant float, usually a plastic ball or block, rests on the water surface and is attached to a lever arm. When cattle drink and the level drops, the float sinks, tilting the arm so it pulls a plunger or washer away from the valve seat. Water then flows into the trough.

As the water rises, the float lifts with it. The lever pushes the plunger back against the seat, gradually narrowing the opening until flow stops at the set level.

Overflow commonly happens when a worn or debris-fouled washer cannot seal against the seat. It also occurs when the float is punctured and waterlogged, so it no longer rises enough to close the valve.
task: Explain how a float valve keeps a livestock water trough filled, what happens as the water level rises, and two ordinary causes of overflow. Use plain accurate prose. Aim for approximately 120–170 English tokens.

text: Preserving an obsolete train timetable offers historians a valuable window into the rhythms of everyday mobility. Beyond listing departures and arrivals, a timetable reveals which towns were connected, how frequently services ran, and how long journeys took, allowing scholars to reconstruct the practical geography of a region at a given moment. Patterns such as early-morning commuter trains, reduced Sunday services, or seasonal excursions suggest how work, leisure, and religious observance structured ordinary lives. Comparing successive editions can also trace broader changes, including suburban growth or rural decline. However, a timetable records planned rather than actual movement: it cannot confirm whether trains ran punctually, how crowded they were, or who travelled. Historians must therefore corroborate it with other evidence, such as passenger accounts, ticket records, or newspapers, to understand lived experience.
task: Discuss in a short academic paragraph how preserving an obsolete train timetable can help historians study everyday mobility; mention one limitation of that source without inventing citations. Aim for approximately 120–170 English tokens.
